title: A hundred days of carp
translation: "A man was telling the old Kitayama chancellor about Lay Monk Sono, who carved fish like nobody else. At some house, a magnificent carp was served. Everyone wanted to see him carve it, but nobody liked to just come out and ask. He knew how to handle that kind of moment, so he said: 'I've been carving a carp every day for a hundred days now, and I can't miss today. Please, let me have this one.' And he carved it. Everyone thought it was just right, and very nicely done.

"But the chancellor said: 'That kind of thing gets on my nerves. If nobody else was going to carve it, he could have said, Give it here, I'll do it. That would have been much better. What's all this about a hundred days of carp?' I thought that was funny."

So do I. On the whole, plain and easy beats clever. When you have guests, it's nice to find some occasion to hang the meal on, but just bringing it out for no reason is better. Same with presents. Give it with no occasion at all and say, "This is for you." That's real kindness. Pretending you can't bear to part with it so they'll have to ask, or handing it over as if you'd lost a bet: that's just tiresome.

{切|き}りぬべき{人|ひと}なくば、たべ、{切|き}らむといひたらむは、{猶|なほ}よかりなむ。
なんでふ{百日|ひやくにち}の{鯉|こひ}を{切|き}らむぞ。』と{宣|のたま}ひたりし、をかしくおぼえし。」と{人|ひと}のかたり{給|たま}ひける、いとをかし。

{賓客|まれびと}の{饗応|きやうおう}なども、ついでをかしき{様|やう}にとりなしたるも、{誠|まこと}によけれども、{唯|ただ}その{事|こと}となくてとり{出|い}でたる、いとよし。

literal: '"The lay monk Sono no Bettō is a carver without equal.
At a certain person's house, a splendid carp was brought out, and everyone wanted to see the lay monk's carving, but hesitated, thinking it would be awkward to bring it up lightly;
the lay monk, being a man of tact, said, "Lately I have been carving a hundred days' carp, and I must not miss today; I humbly ask to be given it", and carved it,
and people thought it very fitting and delightful." When someone told this to the Kitayama lay chancellor,
"That sort of thing I find very tiresome.
If he had said, 'If there is no one who will carve it, give it to me, I will carve it', that would have been better still.
What's this carving of a hundred days' carp?", he said, and I found that amusing,' someone told me: very amusing.
On the whole, being plain and easy without show is better than performing to be interesting.
In entertaining guests too, arranging it so that the occasion is charming is truly good, but bringing something out without any particular reason is very good.
In giving things to people too, saying 'I would like to give you this' without an occasion is true goodwill.
Pretending to be reluctant and hoping to be asked, or making it a pretext of a forfeit for losing a game: that is tiresome.

notes.text: The 1925 edition identifies him as Fujiwara no Motouji (1211–1282), founder of the Sono family, a son of Motoie. This is Jimyōin Motoie, not the Motoie of section 223. {別当|べつたう}: the head of an office, his former post. The reading puts in the unwritten の: そののべつたう.

{庖丁|はうちやう}: the art of carving fish and birds at a banquet, in front of the guests, with a knife and long chopsticks, never touching the food by hand. A {庖丁者|はうちやうじや} is a master of it. Modern {包丁|ほうちょう} 'kitchen knife' comes from this word.
Carp was the most prestigious fish to carve, the only one cut in front of the emperor (see section 118).
A vow to carve a carp every day for a hundred days, as the edition explains. His excuse gives everyone what they wanted without anyone having to ask.
まげて: 'please, even if it is a bother'. {申|まう}しうく: 'to ask for and receive' (humble). A very polite request.

The 1925 edition says Saionji Kintsune (1171–1244). Many modern commentaries take him to be Saionji Sanekane (1249–1322) instead, who also lived at Kitayama (see section 118); some also suggest Kintsune's son Saneuji. {太政|だいじやう}: short for {太政大臣|だいじやうだいじん}, the chancellor, the highest office at court.
The imperative of たぶ 'to give (to me)', as the edition notes. The chancellor's version is short and plain: give it here.
なんでふ: 'what kind of…, what on earth…', from なにといふ. A rough, impatient question.

notes.quote: 人のかたり給ひける、いとをかし
notes.text: The story has three layers: someone tells the chancellor about the carver, the chancellor answers, and someone of rank ({給|たま}ひ) tells the whole thing to Kenkō. Kenkō likes it too.
{負|ま}けわざ: the treat or present the loser of a game or bet must give, as the edition explains. Here the gift is dressed up as a lost bet.
A false friend: むつかし is 'tiresome, unpleasant'. Modern {難|むずか}しい means 'difficult'.
